articles.title: How Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Turns Events Into Reviewable Agent Jobs
articles.excerpt: How Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Turns Events Into Reviewable Agent Jobs AWS's October 2026 walkthrough of Bedrock AgentCore lays out a clean reference pattern for something every agent builder wrestles w…
articles.body: How Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Turns Events Into Reviewable Agent Jobs AWS's October 2026 walkthrough of Bedrock AgentCore lays out a clean reference pattern for something every agent builder wrestles with: how do you let an agent act on real-world events while keeping a human in the loop? The answer is to make everything a job — a persistent, reviewable unit of work. The architecture in brief Event intake: An S3 object-created notification (or a scheduled trigger) hits a Signal Processor Lambda, which matches it against configured signals. Queue: Each match becomes a DynamoDB job record, and execution is decoupled through Amazon SQS — the API never has to stay open while the model thinks.

articles.title: Claude Code and Codex pets: how to get one for every session
articles.excerpt: Codex has pets in two places. In the ChatGPT desktop app, open Settings → Pets, type /pet, or press ⌥Space on macOS to show a floating pet. In an interactive Codex CLI session, type /pets or /pet to c…
articles.body: Codex has pets in two places. In the ChatGPT desktop app, open Settings → Pets , type /pet , or press ⌥Space on macOS to show a floating pet. In an interactive Codex CLI session, type /pets or /pet to choose a terminal pet for that session. Claude Code and Grok Build have no built-in equivalent today. A pet is a small animated companion that shows what your agent is doing: working, waiting for you, done. It is a nice way to keep an eye on an agent without reading its output. Here is how to set one up: In the ChatGPT app: type /pet , choose Show pet from the command menu, or press ⌥Space on macOS. Pick a built-in or custom pet in Settings → Pets . In the Codex CLI: type /pets to pick one, /pets <name> to choose it directly, or /pets off to hide it.

articles.title: Why can you see the moon during the day? This week is the perfect time to find out
articles.excerpt: You don't have to wait until dark to see the moon. Here's why it appears in broad daylight — and why this week is a particularly good time to spot it.
articles.body: I know perfectly well that the moon comes out during the day. I have known this for decades. Yet whenever I spot it in a blue afternoon sky, some primitive part of my brain still thinks it has turned up early. I'm certainly not the only one. Many people don't understand how it could be visible in daylight. In their eyes, the moon is a nighttime object. Why? Because that's when they notice it — it appears brighter. We tend to think of the sun as belonging to the day and the moon to the night because that's how they're usually presented to us as children. Astronomically, it makes little sense. The moon spends plenty of time above our horizon while the sun is also up — it spends half its time in the daytime sky, in fact.

articles.body: I've spent years chasing the northern lights across the Arctic, from the mountains of Swedish Lapland to the dramatic Norwegian fjords. Whether you're on the hunt for somewhere that offers the best chance of clear skies, the most dramatic scenery or a plethora of winter activities to keep you warm, choosing the right destination can make a big difference, especially as auroras are never guaranteed. My biggest piece of advice? Choose somewhere you've always wanted to visit regardless of whether the northern lights might appear. That way, the auroras become the icing on the cake rather than the sole measure of a successful trip.
